title: Karnataka Bans Analogue Paneer for One Year as Four States Crack Down on Dairy Fraud
excerpt: Karnataka joins Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh in prohibiting non-dairy paneer substitutes sold without disclosure at restaurants and food establishments.
body:
• Karnataka has banned the manufacture, sale, and use of analogue paneer for one year, joining Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh in a nationwide crackdown on dairy fraud
  • Analogue paneer, made from vegetable oils and additives instead of milk, was being served as genuine dairy paneer without disclosure in restaurants and hotels
  • In Maharashtra, 35.4% of 308 paneer samples tested over the past year failed quality standards, with 30 declared unsafe
  • Violators face penalties ranging from six months' imprisonment and a Rs 1 lakh fine to life imprisonment if consumption causes death

Karnataka has banned the manufacture and sale of analogue paneer for one year, becoming the latest Indian state to crack down on non-dairy substitutes being passed off as genuine paneer in restaurants, hotels, and retail outlets, according to The Hindu and NDTV.

The state order prohibits the production, sale, and use of analogue paneer — a cheaper substitute made from vegetable oils, starches, emulsifiers, and other additives — that is marketed under the name "paneer." Hotels, restaurants, caterers, cloud kitchens, and eateries across Karnataka are barred from using or stocking the product for the duration of the ban.

A Growing State-by-State Crackdown

Karnataka joins Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh in what has become a coordinated push by Indian states against dairy fraud. Maharashtra's ban, issued through a gazette notification by Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, set the template: a comprehensive prohibition covering the entire supply chain from manufacture to retail.

The Maharashtra action followed a year-long surveillance exercise by the state's Food and Drug Administration. Of 308 paneer and dairy analogue samples analyzed between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 — or 35.4% — failed prescribed standards. Among these, 79 were classified as sub-standard and 30 were declared unsafe. Laboratory testing revealed that natural milk fat was frequently replaced with cheap vegetable oils and non-dairy fats.

"The big question is why fake or duplicate products made with palmolein oil are legally allowed to use dairy names like cheese or paneer. It's like allowing gold-polished brass or aluminium jewellery to use the BIS hallmark logo."

— R.S. Sodhi, Former Managing Director, Amul

Why It Matters for Consumers

Analogue paneer lacks the primary nutritional benefits of genuine dairy paneer — particularly the protein content that millions of vegetarians across India rely on as a dietary staple. The substitute typically contains higher amounts of processed fats and limited quantities of essential vitamins and minerals.

The core consumer concern is deception. Food safety authorities across multiple states have found that restaurants and hotels were serving analogue paneer as conventional dairy paneer without informing customers. This practice has been designated an unfair trade practice under Section 24 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Penalties are severe. Violations can attract imprisonment of six months and a fine of Rs 1 lakh. In cases where consumption of unsafe food results in death, offenders could face life imprisonment and a minimum fine of Rs 10 lakh.

National-Level Action on the Horizon

With four states now banning analogue paneer, pressure is building for a national response. A committee has recommended that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) stop permitting new dairy analogue products altogether. The recommendation calls for no new standards on analogue paneer and for approximately 1,000 existing licence holders to be given time to remove these products from the market.

BJP MLA Vikram Pachpute, who pushed for the Maharashtra ban in the state legislature, has called for extending scrutiny to cheese analogues, arguing that consumers face similar deception with processed cheese products.

What to Watch

For Indians traveling home and for the diaspora community that follows food safety closely, the enforcement landscape is shifting fast. Paneer appears in dishes from palak paneer to paneer tikka in restaurants nationwide. With bans now in effect in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh, establishments in these states are required to serve only genuine dairy paneer.

Jayatheertha Chary, managing director of Mother Dairy, called the bans "a progressive step" that would "strengthen trust in the country's dairy ecosystem." Whether the remaining states follow — and whether the FSSAI acts at the national level — will determine if the current state-by-state approach gives way to a uniform standard. The existing law permits a prohibition of this nature for a maximum of one year, meaning any permanent solution will require changes to food safety regulations.
nri_angle: The crackdown on analogue paneer affects NRIs visiting India who eat at restaurants, and highlights food safety standards that diaspora consumers increasingly track across India's food industry.
